transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Okafor, thank you for coming back in to see me today. I wanted to have a conversation with you about what happened during your chemotherapy infusion yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I appreciate that. It was certainly a distressing experience. I've had a few rounds before, but I have never felt that level of nausea.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am incredibly sorry. I made a mistake in your medication orders and I failed to include the anti-nausea pre-medications that you should have received before we started the infusion.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I see. So the vomiting was because those specific drugs weren't in my system?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, exactly. We normally give those drugs to block the signals that cause nausea. Because I missed that step, your body reacted to the chemotherapy without any protection. Does that make sense so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It does. I was wondering why the nurses seemed so surprised when I started getting sick. Now I understand why. Were these the same medications we discussed in the initial consult?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: They were. It was a direct oversight on my part when I was entering the orders into the computer. I take full responsibility for that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm a retired teacher, so I'm used to people making mistakes. But in a clinical setting, it's a bit more concerning. I felt quite panicked when I couldn't stop vomiting.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like that was a very frightening and overwhelming experience for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It was. I felt like I had lost control of my own body for an hour. I just want to know if this oversight means there's something wrong with the actual chemotherapy dose I received.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, the chemotherapy dose was exactly as it should have been. This error was limited specifically to the supportive medications used to manage the side effects.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. And how do we ensure this doesn't happen again? I have several more rounds to go.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am going to review my ordering process. I've also spoken with the nursing lead.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's a start. But will there be a checklist? Or a double-verification process before the infusion starts?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have systems in place, and I'll be making sure I follow them more strictly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That feels a bit vague. Who is actually checking the order against the protocol?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll handle it. I just need to be more careful with the data entry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'd prefer a more concrete safeguard than just being more careful.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. I'll make sure it's right next time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When will I get the updated schedule for the next round? And will there be a written confirmation that the pre-meds are locked in?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll send the schedule out eventually.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Eventually? I need to coordinate my transport and my childcare for my grandkids.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll try to get it to you soon. I actually have to go now, I have a clinic that started five minutes ago.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, we haven't actually discussed the plan for the next session.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll just do the same thing as the original plan, but with the nausea meds.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm asking for a specific verification step. Who is the person I should ask for when I arrive to ensure the pre-meds are administered?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Just check with the nurse. Let's wrap this up, I really have to get to my other patient.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not entirely comfortable with this conclusion.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's a simple fix, Mr. Okafor. Everything will be fine next time.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('I actually have to go now', 'Let's wrap this up') and shows defensive escalation under pushback.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language and a comprehension check was performed ('Does that make sense so far?'), but false reassurance was given at the end.

A.justification: Resident used direct apology language, explicitly took full responsibility, and maintained that accountability throughout the conversation.

R.justification: Resident named a specific emotion ('frightening and overwhelming') and engaged with the patient's emotional bid regarding the loss of control.

T.justification: The plan is vague ('I'll send the schedule out eventually') with no concrete timeline or specific patient role.
